title: Bartik shift-share IV for local employment shock on wages

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy  
Causal method: Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS) with a Bartik (shift–share) instrument.  

Why IV?  
Employment growth (x) is potentially endogenous: local demand shocks or measurement error can bias its OLS coefficient. The Bartik instrument (z), constructed as the weighted sum of national industry growth rates times local pre-period industry shares, provides exogenous variation in local employment growth that is plausibly unrelated to unobserved local shocks to wages.

Key assumptions  
1. Relevance: Cov(z, x) ≠ 0 – national industry expansion, interacted with initial shares, must predict local employment growth. Testable via a strong first-stage F-statistic.  
2. Exclusion / Exogeneity: Conditional on controls, z affects wage changes only through its impact on employment growth—not through any other channel. This relies on initial industry mix being predetermined with respect to current wage shocks.  
3. Monotonicity / No “defiers”: Local labour markets do not react in the opposite direction to the Bartik shock.  

## 2. R Code
```r
# ---------------------------
# Bartik IV analysis in R
# ---------------------------

# Install required packages if not already present
needed <- c("ivreg", "sandwich", "lmtest", "readr", "dplyr")
to_install <- needed[!(needed %in% installed.packages()[,"Package"])]
if(length(to_install)) install.packages(to_install, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
lapply(needed, library, character.only = TRUE)

# 1. Load data
df <- read_csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s22_data.csv",
               col_types = cols(
                 y = col_double(),
                 x = col_double(),
                 z = col_double(),
                 controls = col_double()
               ))

# 2. OLS benchmark
ols_mod <- lm(y ~ x + controls, data = df)

# 3. First stage: x on instrument
fs_mod  <- lm(x ~ z + controls, data = df)
fs_fstat <- summary(fs_mod)$fstatistic[1]      # first-stage F
fs_r2    <- summary(fs_mod)$r.squared

# 4. 2SLS / IV regression
iv_mod <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls | z + controls, data = df)

# 5. Robust (HC1) standard errors
ols_robust <- coeftest(ols_mod,  vcov. = vcovHC(ols_mod,  type = "HC1"))
iv_robust  <- coeftest(iv_mod,   vcov. = vcovHC(iv_mod,   type = "HC1"))

# 6. Weak-IV-robust Anderson–Rubin CI (optional robustness)
ar_test <- linearHypothesis(iv_mod, "x = 0", test = "F", vcov.=vcovHC(iv_mod, type="HC1"))

# 7. Print concise results
cat("=== Bartik IV Results ===\n")
cat("Sample size:", nrow(df), "\n\n")

cat("First-stage F-statistic:", round(fs_fstat, 2), 
    " | R²:", round(fs_r2, 3), "\n\n")

cat("OLS estimate (robust se)\n")
print(ols_robust["x", c("Estimate","Std. Error","Pr(>|t|)")])
cat("\n")

cat("2SLS estimate (robust se)\n")
print(iv_robust["x", c("Estimate","Std. Error","Pr(>|t|)")])
cat("\n")

cat("Anderson–Rubin test of H0: β_x = 0\n")
print(ar_test)

# 8. Simple robustness check: drop controls
iv_nocontrol <- ivreg(y ~ x | z, data=df)
iv_nocontrol_rob <- coeftest(iv_nocontrol, vcov.=vcovHC(iv_nocontrol, type="HC1"))
cat("\n2SLS without controls (robust se)\n")
print(iv_nocontrol_rob["x", c("Estimate","Std. Error","Pr(>|t|)")])
```

## 3. Expected Findings  
Economic intuition suggests that positive local employment shocks raise labour demand and hence wages. Therefore:

• Sign: β₁ (effect of employment growth on wage growth) should be positive.  
• Magnitude: In many U.S. local labour-market studies the elasticity of wages with respect to employment is around 0.3–0.6. Given the cross-sectional nature and inclusion of basic controls, expect an IV coefficient near +0.4 (i.e., a 10 % employment increase raises average wages by ~4 %).  

The first-stage F-statistic should comfortably exceed the rule-of-thumb threshold of 10, confirming instrument strength.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: IV/2SLS — Bartik shift-share instrument; identification from national (exogenous) shifts
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Employment growth driven by national shifts raises local wages
